10 rare game consoles that almost no one owns

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1584 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Limited editions, sweepstakes rewards and specific game bundle consoles far exceed their initial price.
  • Industry observers note that most people can recognize an original PlayStation or Nintendo 64 at a glance, but some variations of common consoles are much less familiar.
  • If you have an older console tucked away in a closet, it could be worth checking which edition you own.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Limited editions, sweepstakes rewards and specific game bundle consoles far exceed their initial price.

Industry observers note that most people can recognize an original PlayStation or Nintendo 64 at a glance, but some variations of common consoles are much less familiar. Perhaps they were made for a limited promotion, released exclusively in Japan or were given away through a contest. Some consoles never made it to stores, like the Nintendo PlayStation prototype acquired by the National Videogame Museum.

If you have an older console tucked away in a closet, it could be worth checking which edition you own. A system you might have considered to be obsolete and boring could be worth more than you think.

Sources indicate that to gauge how rare these editions are, we looked at production numbers, limited giveaways and collector records. For resale values, we prioritized documented sales and price-guide estimates.

In a recent development, the Nintendo 64 came in plenty of colors (and inspired Analogue 3D colors based on N64 prototypes), but this gold version is one you probably didn't see on store shelves. The Toys "R" Us-exclusive edition featured a metallic gold console with matching controllers, which was much flashier than the usual gray and black hardware.

Recent findings suggest that while it's not a production total, Video Game Authority's (VGA) December 2025 census listed only nine examples of this variant. A gold console graded 80 (out of 100) NM (near-mint) by VGA, with two matching controllers, sold for $3,250 in January 2026. Recent ungraded sales tracked by PriceCharting include loose consoles for around $140 to $425, while those still in the box have sold for $1,750 to $3,000 in 2026.

If you grew up during the Pokémon '90s boom, you might remember the Pikachu Edition Nintendo 64; it was released as a Toys "R" Us exclusive in North America. The console came in blue and yellow with a raised Pikachu on top, a Poké Ball-shaped power button and matching controller. The set also included Hey You, Pikachu! and the Voice Recognition Unit needed to play it.

A sealed example graded VGA 80+ sold for $10,000 in May 2025, and another sealed example graded VGA 80+ fetched $16,250 in August 2026. Both were complete collector sets, so don't mistake those prices for what a regular used console is worth. For a more everyday comparison, PriceCharting's estimates put a loose Pikachu N64 around $390 and a complete set at roughly $1,567.

Heritage reported 22 sealed examples in VGA's April census, with only one graded higher than the example sold in May 2025.

According to recent reports, in 2000, Sony gave away a Midnight Blue edition of the original PlayStation through a sweepstakes. Just 100 consoles were available in North America, along with 1,000 DualShock controllers. Japan had its own promotion, with another 100 consoles offered as contest prizes to mark the anticipated milestone of 10 million PlayStation units sold domestically. The reported total across both promotions was 200 consoles.

These are hard to price because they're rarely on the market. PriceCharting demonstrates an eBay sale for a 10 Million model PlayStation at $10,326.32 in October 2024. There are reported private sales of $9,000 in 2021 and $3,000 in 2017. Its current guide estimates a complete-in-box example at about $9,663, while its estimates for fresh and graded-new examples are much higher ($25,000 and above).

The GameCube had a great library of games, but it couldn't play DVDs. To remedy this, Panasonic made the Q, a Japan-exclusive system that combined GameCube hardware with a DVD player. It released in Japan on December 14, 2001, for ¥39,800, or about $325 at the time. Its silver finish, front-panel LCD and DVD playback made it an unusual hybrid for the era.

Recent findings suggest that by December 2003, Panasonic had stopped production. It was still priced at ¥34,800 (about $324), compared with ¥13,800 (about $128) for the standard GameCube. The Q is one of several unusual GameCube systems collectors seek out.

In a recent development, priceCharting's records include working systems selling for $800 to $2,200 in 2026, depending on condition, accessories and modifications. Its current guide estimates a loose system at about $1,645, a complete set with its box and accessories at around $2,200, and a sealed, ungraded system at about $4,569. A sealed example graded VGA 80 sold for $7,512 in December 2024.

Sega gave its Saturn a see-through makeover with the Skeleton Edition. It launched in Japan on April 4, 1998, with a translucent gray shell and a matching transparent controller. Sega limited the release to 30,000 units. The tech giant also released a separate Skeleton Saturn bundle with Derby Stallion in March 1999. That's a different variant, so check the model and bundle details before comparing prices.

It has been revealed that the console originally sold for ¥20,000 in Japan. PriceCharting lists a loose system at about $430, a complete-in-box set at around $573, and a upcoming example at roughly $900. Recent sales include a tested console that sold for $439 in September 2026, while a boxed example sold for $530 in May 2026. Another tested system with its controller, cables and box sold for $429.99 in March 2026.

In a recent development, most Dreamcast consoles came in white, but the Japan-exclusive Maziora Edition (named for a popular Japanese paint) shifted between green and purple depending on the light and angle. This isn't confirmed by Sega, but collector databases report that just 500 Maziora consoles were made, with around 200 signed by Japanese racing driver Tadahiko Taira.

Industry observers note that priceCharting doesn't have enough completed sales to estimate a price guide for this variant. Its rarity makes it difficult to establish a reliable current market value, and available eBay listings don't provide enough verifiable sales information to determine what buyers are actually paying.

In a recent development, this Dreamcast was made for Resident Evil (known as Biohazard in Japan) fans, but it wasn't easy to get your hands on. It was released in Japan along with Biohazard Code: Veronica in February 2000. The limited-edition bundle included a Dreamcast, matching controller, Visual Memory Unit and the game itself.

Fans entered a raffle to get one, and the console they received was up to chance. Capcom produced 2,000 bundles, but only 200 featured the blue S.T.A.R.S. console. The other 1,800 came in translucent pink, inspired by Claire Redfield.

Industry observers note that the original bundle retailed for ¥34,800, or about $340 at the time. Given the limited production run and the small number of blue consoles, it's difficult to establish a reliable current market value from documented sales, though there is one at the moment listed for $18,000.

For the original Xbox's second anniversary in Japan, Microsoft swapped its black casing for a white finish with silver accents. The Pure White Limited Edition ran just 1,000 units and wasn't sold in regular stores. Buyers had to order through the official Xbox Japan website during a one-week window in early 2004.

Sources indicate that the console originally retailed for ¥19,800 (about $186) and came with a white controller, DVD playback kit and Xbox Live starter kit. It also included a one-year Xbox Live membership and a voice communicator (headset). You could personalize the console with a short name or message engraved on its casing.

In a recent development, it's now worth considerably more than its original price. PriceCharting records a complete example selling for $1,599 in May 2026, another for $2,651.11 in March 2026, and a near-mint complete set for $1,999.99 in January 2026. Its current guide estimates a complete set at around $2,100 and a upcoming example at about $2,551.

Recent findings suggest that sony released a PS4 Pro in 2018 that let you see straight into its hardware, commemorating half a billion sales across all PlayStation models. The 500 Million Limited Edition featured a translucent dark-blue shell, copper-colored accents and a matching controller, with a numbered copper plate on each console. Sony made just 50,000 worldwide, each with a 2TB hard drive.

Recent findings suggest that the console originally retailed for $499.99 in the US and rolled out on August 24, 2018. Sony has continued releasing commemorative hardware, including its PlayStation 30th Anniversary limited-edition PS5 consoles, which pay tribute to the original PlayStation.

Industry observers note that this edition has a pretty active resale market. PriceCharting shows completed sales of $500 in March 2026 and $750 in September 2026. The site's current guide estimates a loose system at about $550, a complete example at $750, and a fresh console at around $1,325.

In a recent development, this is an Xbox that Microsoft never meant to sell to the general public, as the translucent green Launch Team Edition was made for the people behind the original Xbox in 2001. It features Bill Gates' signature on the center jewel, along with the message "Great Work!" and a "Special Edition" label on the front. It also came with two translucent green Duke controllers that weren't sold separately. Microsoft has revived the translucent-green look for its 25th anniversary Xbox Series X and matching controller.

It's not confirmed exactly how many were made. LCG Auctions estimates around 1,000 consoles, while collector databases estimate between 1,000 and 5,000. The price can vary widely depending on what's included. One example with the Bill Gates signature sold for $967.20 at LCG Auctions in August 2025. PriceCharting shows another console sale for $3,000 in March 2026, and lists a complete example at an estimated $6,999.99.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • While Apple's white earbuds look similar, the AirPods 5 and AirPods Pro 3 differ in design, charging options, capabilities and battery life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The cheaper AirPods 5 have less capabilities than the AirPods Pro 3.

While Apple's white earbuds look similar, the AirPods 5 and AirPods Pro 3 differ in design, charging options, capabilities and battery life. The AirPods 5 come in two options (the base $129 model and the $149 model), while the Apple AirPods Pro 3 have one option that costs $249.

Sources indicate that let's begin with the differences in appearances. AirPods 5 have a slightly more oval-shaped bud and are solid earbuds without ear tips, designed to pop inside your ear and fit with a gentle twist. AirPods Pro 3 carry replaceable silicon ear tips that seal themselves inside the ear canal. The seal improves music playback fidelity and blocks more external noise. AirPods Pro 3 include five ear tip sizes so you can find the right fit, though other options exist, particularly for smaller ears.

Industry observers note that before diving into more differences, these products do have some similarities. Both AirPods support Active Noise Cancellation (ANC), partly through latest multiport acoustic architecture on AirPods 5. Both models use Apple's H2 chip which improves music playback and powers popular features. These include Personalized Spatial Audio with head tracking, Voice Isolation and studio-quality recording, Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, and Live Translation, when available. Both offer IP57 durability: they are dust resistant and should continue to work if submerged in up to 1 meter (3.3 feet) of fresh water for a short time.

According to recent reports, apple promises that the $129 AirPods 5 will keep going for up to four hours on one charge with ANC active (five hours with the $149 set). AirPods Pro 3 earbuds provide eight hours of music playback with ANC.

It has been revealed that airPods have always shipped with a protective case that doubles up as charging stations for the buds. You'll get an hour of playback if you put them in the case for 5 minutes.

It has been revealed that there's a difference in the battery capacity provided by the cases. The entry-level AirPods 5 case provides 20 hours and powers over USB-C. The $149 model reaches 22 hours and supports wireless charging. AirPods Pro 3 also offer both wireless and USB-C charging and promise 24 hours of battery life.

Sources indicate that one final difference concerns Apple's Find My system which will help you track down a lost set of AirPods. With both AirPods, cases that support wireless charging also carry speakers that can make a noise to help you find them when mislaid. The case provided with the $129 AirPods 5 lacks this. Find My is improved with AirPods Pro 3, which supports precise tracking.

Industry observers note that if you need Active Noise Cancellation (ANC) to suppress external noise, you're in luck, as both AirPods variants provide it. However, AirPods Pro 3 are more efficient because they use silicon ear tips which seal the ear canal, blocking external noise.

Recent findings suggest that airPods Pro 3 provide some unique health-related features you don't find in AirPods 5, too. For example, AirPods Pro 3 provide heart rate sensing during workouts, which AirPods 5 do not. They also offer regulatory-approved hearing-related features: The short Hearing Test builds a profile for your hearing which the Hearing Aid feature uses to amplify external sound for people with hearing loss.

Another difference is that you can swipe the stalk of the AirPods to increase or lower volume on AirPods Pro 3 and the $149 AirPods 5 but not on the entry-level $129 Airpods 5.

Sources indicate that summing up, if you want efficient ANC, excellent music playback and sophisticated health features, choose the AirPods Pro 3. Otherwise, you'll get more from the $149 AirPods 5 than from the base $129 model.

Breaking: GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them.
  • The global food system is ultimately driven by demand.
  • With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.

The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade, and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access.

With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land—an area slightly larger than Italy—for other uses.

The biggest effects, however, occurred when reduced calorie intake was combined with a shift toward healthier diets. In this scenario, up to 7 million deaths could be avoided each year by 2050, while around 46 million hectares of agricultural land would have become available for other uses. This suggests that alongside weight-loss medicines, we need to make healthier options more widely available, affordable, and more appealing.

Industry observers note that food systems are interconnected across countries. If demand falls in one part of the world, this can affect farming, trade, and food prices elsewhere, with consequences for people who are not taking the medications at all.

Industry observers note that lower demand from GLP-1 users, for instance, could make food cheaper. That sounds positive, but cheaper food could also encourage greater consumption among non-users, offsetting some of the intended benefit. The effects of widespread GLP-1 use, in other words, cannot be understood just by looking at individual patients’ weight loss. They ripple through the global food system.

It’s tempting to read these findings as an argument for putting more people on weight-loss medication. That would miss the bigger picture.

Obesity has often been framed as a “lifestyle disease,” blaming individual people for not having enough willpower. But diets are shaped by what food is available, what it costs, how it’s marketed, where shops are located, and what’s most convenient. In many high-income countries, it is remarkably easy to consume large amounts of cheap, energy-dense food. Society tells people to make healthier choices while surrounding them with an environment that often encourages the opposite.

The UK government-commissioned national food strategy, finalized in 2021, made this point clearly: improving diets can’t simply be about asking individuals to choose better. The wider food environment needs to change to make the better choice the easy one.

Industry observers note that our findings shouldn’t be taken to mean that people living with obesity have a responsibility to lose weight to reduce the environmental impacts of food production. Rather, our research examines the wider consequences that changes in food demand could have across the food system.

A healthier diet is not necessarily just a diet with fewer calories. It could mean more fruit, vegetables, and other nutritious foods, alongside less excessive consumption of foods linked to poor health. These changes affect not only human health but also agriculture, land use, and the environment.

In a recent development, rather than asking whether GLP-1 medications or healthier diets are the answer, let’s ask how they can work together. Imagine a food system where healthier foods are affordable and accessible, unhealthy options aren’t relentlessly promoted, agricultural policy supports nutritious and sustainable production, and people who need medical treatment can access it. That combination could be far more powerful than any single intervention.

Industry observers note that GLP-1 medicines can play an important role in tackling obesity, but they shouldn’t become a technological fix that allows the wider food system to escape scrutiny. They can help people eat less in an unhealthy food environment, but the long-term goal should be to make it easier and more affordable to have a healthier, more sustainable diet.

The remarkable thing about GLP-1 medications may not be that they change how much food people eat. It may be that they show us, with new clarity, just how closely human health, food production, and environmental health are connected, and how much could be gained if we tackled all three together.

Roslyn Henry is Lecturer, School of Biological Sciences, University of Aberdeen and Peter Alexander is Professor of Global Food Systems, University of Edinburgh.

After I published my review of the HomeView, Apple’s first smart display, y’all still had a ton of questions about how it works as a smart speaker. So, I spent a bunch more time testing its audio capabilities and support for third-party music apps — and found a few more frustrations along the way. Here are the answers to all your burning questions. Have more? I’ll answer them in the comments.

The HomeView isn’t a replacement for a Sonos One, a full-size HomePod, or a similar-size speaker. Those are much better speakers. In size and sound, the HomeView is closer to the HomePod Mini. I tested it alongside the Mini 2 (which sounds marginally better than the first-gen Mini) and found the tabletop HomeView mostly comparable, with these caveats: The HomeView has better bass and is slightly louder, but it’s not as clear and is less room-filling.

You can hear them both in action in this video, alongside the full-size HomePod, the Sonos One, and the wall-mounted HomeView:.

The difference comes down to the hardware. The Mini 2 has a single full-range driver and two passive radiators, whereas the tabletop HomeView has two drivers in the display, plus a woofer and two passive radiators in its base. While the woofer adds some oomph, the HomeView’s display, which sits over the speaker base, partly covers it, affecting the sound compared to the Mini. Apple added an accelerometer to the display because tilting it changes the sound, so HomeView adjusts its EQ in real time based on the angle. Still, the Mini, while not as loud, fills a room better, thanks partly to its 360-degree sound. (The HomeView supports Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos, which the Mini 2 doesn’t.).

It has been revealed that the wall-mounted HomeView has only two drivers, with computational audio Apple claims is “tuned specifically for on-wall placement.” It sounds fine but is noticeably thinner than the tabletop version, and bass is basically non-existent. I wouldn’t recommend it for its sound quality, but it’s great for talking to a visitor through your video doorbell.

No. While you can group HomeViews with any other AirPlay speakers to play music out of them all at once, you can’t pair two for a stereo setup or pair a HomeView with a HomePod or Mini. I like the sound of two Minis paired in stereo and use this setup in my office and my bedroom. They also work as speakers for my Apple TVs in those rooms.

In a recent development, if you have $300 to spend on a good-sounding smart speaker setup, go with two Minis over a HomeView. The HomeView’s real benefit is the screen. I cover its uses extensively in my full review, but for audio in particular, I like that the screen acts like a jukebox, making it easy to change songs, select upcoming music, and scroll through your podcasts or audiobooks — without needing to find a quarter! With a HomePod, you rely on Siri voice control or your Apple device to select content.

You can AirPlay to the HomeView as with any other AirPlay speaker, and audio handoff works the same as it does on HomePods. Tap your phone to the HomeView, and whatever is playing transfers to the speakers and the screen. Handoff also works in reverse, letting you send any content back to your phone. One addition with the HomeView: You can now hand off video.

In a recent development, in testing, handoff worked for Apple TV, Apple Music, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, Pocket Casts, YouTube Music, FaceTime, and phone calls — although phone calls sometimes dropped. YouTube and YouTube TV videos also handed off, even though they don’t have an app on the HomeView. But Netflix and Amazon Prime Video only played audio, though both played video in the Safari browser.

One word of caution: Handoff is aggressive. As with HomePods, if you’re holding your phone within a few inches, the HomeView will try to hand off content.

HomeView doesn’t let you set a default speaker or group to use instead of its built-in speaker. However, you can play audio to any AirPlay speaker or group of speakers. I tested this on HomePods, Sonos speakers, and a Samsung TV, and it worked smoothly.

According to recent reports, for native apps (Apple Music, Podcasts, and Safari), the HomeView remembers the last speaker or speaker pair you used and automatically plays content through those when you return. If it’s been a while since you opened the app, it pops up the option to choose the last-used speakers.

Spotify has no search box because you’re not supposed to type while driving — only I’m not driving; I’m in my kitchen!

Things get messier with third-party audio apps such as Spotify and Audible, and with Apple apps that use the CarPlay interface, such as Apple News and Apple TV. The HomeView only automatically uses the last speakers if you choose content from the HomeView screen. If you use Siri voice control, it defaults to the HomeView speaker.

According to recent reports, so, “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan from Spotify” played music from HomeView’s speaker and not the stereo pair of Minis in my office, where I’d last been listening to Spotify. I could direct it to play music there by adding “on Office,” but that’s more of a mouthful than just “Hey Siri, play ‘Femininomenon’ by Chappell Roan,” which is all you need to say if you use Apple Music.

Which brings me to another one of your most-asked questions — and my biggest complaint about this device as a smart speaker: How does it support third-party audio apps? Like second-class citizens.

Spotify works on the HomeView, but with limitations that apply to all non-native and third-party apps: they only show up when your phone is connected to the HomeView via your profile, so only you can use them.

It has been revealed that apple has taken a shortcut here: Rather than building a dedicated HomeView experience for app developers, the HomeView uses Apple’s existing CarPlay platform. This makes it easier for developers to put their apps on the HomeView — if an audio or video app supports CarPlay, it already works on the HomeView (there’s no support for other types of CarPlay apps).

According to recent reports, in practice, this creates frustrating limitations, including no search function and the need for a user profile on the HomeView and your phone on the same Wi-Fi. It also results in slower performance and a laggy, inconsistent experience compared to the native apps.

According to recent reports, I tried several apps: Pocket Casts, Amazon Music, YouTube Music, Spotify, and Audible. They all appeared in my HomeView app drawer, and I could access them, choose content via streamlined interfaces, and then play audio on the HomeView or AirPlay from it to any speakers.

According to recent reports, but CarPlay apps don’t work as well as the built-in audio apps — Music, Podcasts, and Safari. They take longer to load and respond more slowly. You also can’t type a search query in any of them, as you can in the native apps, because they don’t have a search field or keyboard. Instead, you have to scroll through content to find what you want or use Siri voice search.

Me: “Siri, resume my Audible book.” Siri: “Shuffling latest songs from Apple Music.”.

According to recent reports, there’s no search box because you’re not supposed to type while driving; only I’m not driving — I’m in my kitchen! This indicates how much of a CarPlay port the apps are; they haven’t been updated to account for the fact that this device is stationary and in your home. Case in point, when I first pulled up the Apple TV app (the only CarPlay video app presently supported), a warning popped up telling me to make sure I was stationary before watching any video.

In a recent development, playing audio through CarPlay apps is also buggy. It didn’t always bring up the music control screen, so I had to use my iPhone to control it. Plus, the Audible app often refused to load at all and didn’t work with Siri voice search. Me: “Siri, resume my Audible book.” Siri: “Shuffling latest songs from Apple Music.”.

CarPlay support feels like a stopgap, and Apple needs to work with developers to refine the software and add HomeView-specific controls for a better, more integrated experience.

Industry observers note that much of the confusion around the HomeView stems from treating it like a smart speaker when it’s really a smart display. I get it; I’ve spent the last decade frustrated by smart displays from Google and Amazon that promise a lot but rarely do it all well.

Industry observers note that if you don’t care about the other features of a smart display and just want a smart speaker, then the reason to buy a HomeView over a HomePod is if you have a use for it as a touchscreen music controller. This lets anyone in the household easily browse and control what’s playing. Bear in mind, though, Apple Music (with a subscription) is the only app anyone can use to play music on the HomeView, as CarPlay apps require a user profile.

If you want a smart speaker primarily to play music and are happy using your voice or phone to control it, go for a HomePod. If you use Spotify or other third-party music services, consider an Echo Dot or Google Home smart speaker; both let you set a default speaker and a default music provider — such as Spotify.

Industry observers note that if you already own HomePods and use Apple Music, the HomeView’s touchscreen will fit in nicely as a simple way to control audio. Just don’t buy one expecting it to fully replace a dedicated smart speaker.

Whether planning a country-hopping odyssey or a quick business trip, your journey will go more smoothly with the best travel adapters that allow you to safely charge all your gadgets wherever you land. After many work trips and family vacations I’ve tested several—both universal and basic options—and my favorites will work in most parts of the world.

The best adapters make great gifts for travelers and deserve a place in your carry-on, but check out our other travel guides, like the Best Travel Essentials, Best Travel Tech for Families, Best Travel Pillows, and Best USB-C Cables.

Updated November 2026: I added a Mukiya travel charger and a Mophie Travel Kit, removed some discontinued devices, and updated links and prices.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a ton to like about this 100-watt universal travel adapter from reliable travel brand Ceptics. It covers more than 200 countries and can charge multiple gadgets in a hurry. The classic slider design pushes out EU, UK, and US plugs, and you can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia and China. I love how securely the plugs lock into place; you must press down firmly to slide them back. You have a universal input socket, an additional side socket for US or Japan plugs, and two USB-C ports and two USB-A ports on the bottom. But what makes this travel adapter my favorite is the retractable USB-C cable. It’s around 25 inches long, the end sticks to the adapter magnetically, and it saves you from having to pack an extra cord. The cable can deliver up to 100 watts in total. The USB-C ports support up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports go up to 12 watts.

Recent findings suggest that for all of its strengths, though, it does provide an unfortunate lack of any grounding. Grounding is meant to reduce the risk of an electric shock if there’s a fault, such as a loose wire inside a device with a metal case. (This video explains grounding well.) Thankfully, there’s overload protection with a 10-amp fuse, and it also comes with a spare. But you should not use this adapter with any device with a third metal ground pin on its plug.

It has been revealed that I also tested the 140-watt Ceptics 6-in-1 model ($51), which omits the cable but has three USB-C ports and one USB-A, and the excellent 70-watt model ($40), which has the retractable cable but fewer ports and loses the extra outlet. Both are great alternatives.

It has been revealed that perhaps the smallest travel adapter that's still practical to use, the Epicka Air measures 3.46 x 1.97 inches and is just 1.19 inches thick, with the prongs folded away. It’s easy to pack but still feels reasonably sturdy in use. You get one USB-A and three USB-C ports. The first three ports offer up to 15 watts apiece, and the last USB-C port on the right can go up to 65 watts. But 65 watts is also the maximum output across the four ports, so it gets divided if you plug in multiple devices. But if you use the AC outlet too, and you can charge up to five devices at once.

When I first tested the 40-watt version ($25), I wasn’t sure about this travel adapter, but after using the 65-watt model for a while, I’ve grown to like it. I still think this style of folding design can be a bit fiddly to use, and the prongs sometimes fold back if you bump them while plugging in. But the placement of the EU prongs in the middle helps it stay plugged in more reliably than some larger sliding cube adapters; the US prongs lock into place, and I didn’t have any problems with the UK prongs.

This budget Ceptics device proves that you don’t need to spend that much money to snag one of the best travel adapters. It covers more than 150 countries, with sliders you push to reveal the three most common international plugs—EU, UK, and US. You can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia or China. The sliders lock into place securely, and there’s a button on the side for retracting them. This plug’s universal outlet can recharge your power-hungry devices, like laptops and camera batteries. Two USB-C and two USB-A ports on the bottom, plus a USB-C port on the side, can handle phones, tablets, smartwatches, and Kindles. Each USB-C port can deliver up to 15 watts, and each USB-A port up to 12 watts. While it's not as fast as some of my picks above, you won't care if you tend to charge your gadgets overnight.

Sources indicate that there’s no grounding, so don’t plug devices with a third metal ground pin into this adapter. There is an 8-amp fuse for safety, and it comes with a spare. It is also certified by RoHS and CE.

In a recent development, what I love about this sturdy, compact plug adapter is the lack of sliding pins or moving parts to worry about. It stays put in the outlet. Offered in several versions (Type C, Type E/F, Type G), this adapter enables you to charge up to six gadgets. I’ve been testing the Type G model in Scotland, and it plugs into a single outlet, giving you three US outlets, a USB-A port, and two USB-C ports. The USB-C can output up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports are limited to 12 watts—not especially speedy, but fine for overnight charging. The adapter is grounded and has various safety features.

In a recent development, on the downside, it can be tough to use all the outlets simultaneously, as larger plugs, like the MacBook power adapter, tend to block one of the other US outlets. It does not offer surge protection, and the Type G adapter maxes out at 3,250 watts (250 volts, 13 amps), while the EU and other versions top out at 2,500 watts.

If you only need USB-C and USB-A ports for charging your mobile gadgets on the go (and no outlet), I recommend this clever, compact travel adapter. I’ve never seen a mechanism like this before, where you twist to extend the prongs. It's a neat feature. The standard US prongs can be angled for Australia, and there are EU and UK prongs (types A, C, G, and I). The USB-C ports can deliver up to 70 watts, enough to charge a laptop (slowly), and there’s a USB-A port. You could charge up to three devices at once, though the wattage is divided between them, and it got a little warm when I did this. It uses gallium nitride (GaN) technology to keep the size down. This is a fresh brand to me, but I’ve been testing it on various devices for the last two weeks, and so far, so good.

In a recent development, universal adapters don't always work properly everywhere, and most don’t have grounding. The cheaper and more reliable alternative is to buy individual adapters. The 12-piece international set from Ceptics is my favorite. It includes types to cover most of the globe, and each is properly grounded. Only visiting a single destination? Just pack the relevant type. These adapters don't have USB ports, so you’ll need the respective charging adapter for your gadgets.

This set is especially good for Europe because it includes Type C, E/F, and G adapters, so you’re covered for any socket. Ceptics offers an even cheaper and smaller five-piece set, but I don’t recommend it. The adapters are flimsy, there’s no grounding, and the European plug’s design doesn’t work well with the recessed sockets you will sometimes encounter. The drawback of plug adapters is that they’re easy to lose, but at least Ceptics includes a small bag for storage.

This kit includes multiple plug attachments that slide and lock into place to keep you powered across most of the world. It is bulky and much bigger than the average adapter but provides two grounded US AC outlets. There is also a built-in USB-C cable, two USB-A ports, and two USB-C ports. The USB-A ports and built-in USB-C cable offer a combined maximum charging rate of 15 watts. The USB-C ports support Power Delivery, with up to 20 watts each. The top charging rate for all of them simultaneously is 55 watts.

Industry observers note that there is built-in surge protection, but since this is not a voltage converter, don’t plug in hair dryers or other non-dual-voltage electronics. While the two AC outlets are handy, their proximity means that the shape and size of some plugs can make it tricky to use both simultaneously. But with the ability to charge up to seven devices, this kit is handy. I also like the original Ceptics World Travel Adapter Kit ($35), though it lacks the two USB-C ports.

This cute kit comes in a zippered pouch and includes everything you need for a trip. There’s a fold-out charger with a tiltable magnetic Qi2 25W pad for your iPhone or Qi2 Android phone, a 7.5W pad for an Apple Watch, and a 5W pad behind for wireless earbuds. It also includes a 40W power adapter with switchable plugs for the US, UK, EU, and AU—plus a 5-foot USB-C cable. Everything inside comes in color-matched black or cream, unless you opt for the bolder orange-and-teal special edition.

According to recent reports, it’s not the most compact option, but I love that everything slots neatly into the included pouch. You can find some great alternatives in my Best Apple 3-in-1 Travel Chargers guide.

What Type of Adapter Do You Need?

According to recent reports, there are 15 plug types in use across the world. Universal adapters tend to cover all of these types.

Some countries are not usually covered by universal adapters, such as India (Type D), Israel (Type H), and South Africa (Type M or N). You'll need to buy specific plug adapters for those places. To avoid any surprises when you land, double-check what type you need before you travel.

Recent findings suggest that if you're visiting just one destination, a basic plug adapter that caters to one plug type is all you need. For trips to multiple destinations or for frequent flyers, a universal travel adapter can prove more versatile. The universal adapters I recommend here have the bonus of including multiple USB ports for charging several mobile devices from a single outlet.

Do You Really Need a Voltage Converter?

Recent findings suggest that voltage converters are big, heavy, and expensive, and they don’t always work—so it’s probably best to avoid them. The reason you might think you need one is that the AC sockets on all of our recommended travel adapters do not convert the voltage coming from the socket. This means plugging into a UK socket will deliver 220 volts at 50 hertz, which is very different from the 120 volts at 60 hertz you can expect in the US. Don't worry! Your gear won’t get fried. You just need to make sure anything you plug into one of these universal travel adapters has something like this printed on it:.

That should include most modern gadgets. If your device or charger can’t handle a variable voltage, it’s probably best to leave it at home. Most places provide hair dryers, irons, and kettles, so there’s no need to take them with you. It’s also often cheaper to buy a set with the correct plug at your destination and save the luggage space and hassle.

If you are determined to try a voltage converter (again, I don’t recommend doing so), the Ceptics 2,000-watt Travel Voltage Converter ($70) seems to work well. It has a special 2,000-watt outlet for hair dryers, but only ones that work via a mechanical switch (anything with an electronic circuit board for automatic switch-off or temperature control won’t work and is at risk of being fried if plugged in). It also has two outlets that go up to 200 watts, one USB-C port, and three USB-A ports, though the ports do not support fast charging.

It has been revealed that travel adapters and chargers usually state the wattage they can deliver for USB-C and USB-A ports, retractable cables, and wireless charging. If you're interested in getting the fastest rates possible, you’ll want a charger and cable that can deliver the maximum wattage to your device. A laptop might want 100 watts, while a phone only needs 30 watts. There's no need to worry if the charger can deliver more wattage than is required because the device will dictate how much power to draw. If the wattage is lower than required, most devices will simply charge slowly. You can find out more about charging standards like Power Delivery (PD), Quick Charge (QC), and others in my guide on how to fast charge your phone.

Can Travel Adapters Go in a Suitcase?

Recent findings suggest that yes, you can pack travel adapters in your suitcase. It may be wise to bring one in your hand luggage for easy access should you need to charge up a device when you arrive at your destination. In fact, devices like power banks with lithium batteries (must be capped at 27,000 mAh) must go in hand luggage, not checked bags.

Can I Buy Travel Adapters at the Airport or Hotel?

You certainly can buy travel adapters at the airport, but like all other goods you buy at kiosks between connecting flights, they will be far more expensive than necessary, and your choice will be limited.

Some hotels have travel adapters, and some even have wall outlets for other countries (or USB-A and USB-C ports), but most do not, so don’t bank on it. You can always check with your hotel or accommodation before you depart, but it’s safer to bring a travel adapter with you.

Should You Test Your Travel Adapter Before You Go?

Seriously, nothing is worse than thinking you’re being very clever by packing light only to get to your hotel and discover that your gadgets refuse to charge. Between the adapter, cable, and your device, plenty can go wrong, so do a quick test on your wall outlet at home with everything you are taking before you set off on an international trip.

Anytime I fly for work or vacation, I take a few travel adapters and chargers with me to test. I also test them for longer periods at home in the UK. I have power stations and power strips with US and EU outlets to test those plugs. I test each charger with a variety of devices (iPhone, Pixel, iPad, MacBook, AirPods). I try charging with every port and outlet simultaneously to see if the charger gets warm. I assess the charging rates, durability, size, weight, and usability of each device. If there are any special features, I test them too.

There is an endless amount of travel adapters out there you could buy. While I wholeheartedly recommend one of the options above, there are some other travel adapters I've tested that just barely miss the mark.

Epicka Pulse for $30: The beveled edges of this travel adapter from Epicka make it more comfortable to hold. The sliders work well and lock in place securely to cover you in around 200 countries. A pair of USB-C and two USB-A ports provide a good mix of port options. This adapter can deliver up to 45 watts from either USB-C port, while the USB-A ports top out at 18 watts. I also tested the newer Epicka Pulse Duo ($130), which can deliver up to 140 watts across three USB-C and one USB-A ports, has an extra US or Japanese socket in the side and boasts a smart display that shows you the current charging status, wattage, and temperature. Cool as it is, it's overkill for most folks and kinda pricey.

Tessan Travel Adapter 009 for $20: This is a similar design to the Epicka Air I recommend above, but the prongs don’t stay in place as securely when unfolded, and you can only draw a maximum of 20 watts from the one USB-A and two USB-C ports. But it is affordable and compact. Tessan also makes good, traditional, slider universal adapters: There's a 140-watt model ($70), and the most powerful travel adapter I’ve tested, the Voyager 205 ($128), which has six USB-C ports and one USB-A to deliver up to 205 watts. If you don’t care about charging speed, Tessan's 20W model ($23) is very reasonably priced and offers two USB-A and two USB-C ports in a small package.

UGreen Travel Plug Adapter for £17: This travel adapter is for UK folks visiting Europe, and it’s a solid option with a fixed plug (no mechanism). It has only two USB-A and one USB-C port for smaller devices, and it’s very bulky. I prefer the OneBeat above for this type of design.

Statik SmartCharge Pro for $80: This is a nice combo device that includes a 15,000 mAh power bank and a 60-watt wall charger. There are fold-out US prongs and slide-on adapters for the UK, EU, and AU. You also get one USB-A port, one USB-C port, a fold-out USB-C cable, and a wireless charging pad on top that works with your iPhone or Apple Watch.

In a recent development, D-Link 65W Multi-Port GaN Charger (DCP-651) for $30: If two USB-C ports and a USB-A port are enough for your travel needs, this affordable D-Link charger could be for you. It comes with interchangeable plugs for different countries. The 65-watt limit is enough for overnight charging a laptop and a couple of smartphones.

Arsmel VisaPro All-in-One Travel Adapter for $80: This chunky power adapter can charge laptops or multiple small devices with a whopping 170-watt maximum output. It works with any outlet in the US, UK, or EU, thanks to sliding plugs that slot in securely, and you can spin the prongs on the US plug to support the total number of countries (more than 200). I love the mecha-inspired paint job, too. There are four ports along the bottom: two USB-C ports rated at 140 watts, with the third USB-C and USB-A ports rated at 18 watts. It supports PD 3.1, QC 3.0, PPS, FCP, and SCP, and has a 10-amp fuse.

It has been revealed that satechi GaN Travel Charger for $120: If you only take small gadgets with you when you travel, a compact, multi-port wall charger is all you need and a great way to pack light. It plugs directly into the wall and comes with four interchangeable travel adapters for the EU, UK, and Australia, plus a mesh bag to store them. There are four USB-C ports that you can plug your gadgets into, including laptops like the MacBook Pro, tablets, phones, and wearables. With support for Power Delivery 3.1, the first two ports can supply up to 140 watts, and the bottom two ports up to 45 watts. However, the maximum output when all four ports are in use is 145 watts.

In a recent development, baseus 70W Universal Travel Adapter With Retractable Cable for $40: This excellent travel adapter is almost identical to our top pick from Ceptics, offering up to 70 watts, sliding prongs to cover more than 200 countries, and a built-in retractable USB-C cable, not to mention a USB-C port and two USB-A ports. It also has a snazzy black-and-yellow finish. It only misses out because it’s slightly more expensive, but if you can snag one on sale or prefer the colors, it’s a solid option.

Epicka Universal Travel Adapter for $20: This travel adapter from Epicka is still a solid option. The sliding plugs cover 150 countries, and there are four USB-A ports on the bottom and a 15-watt USB-C port on the side. There’s also an 8-amp fuse with a spare, and this adapter is RoHS-, CE-, and FCC-certified.

Sources indicate that masterplug Visitor to UK Travel Adapter (3 Pack) for £12: For visitors to the UK, this simple trio of adapters accepts European, American, Australian, and Asian plugs. They are single-outlet adapters with 13-amp fuses inside, and they work perfectly. These are the adapters I use for long-term testing of devices from the US and elsewhere that lack UK plugs. If you forgot to buy an adapter before arriving in the UK, you can find this affordable three-pack at any Argos store.

In a recent development, anker European Travel Plug Adapter for $16: One of our favorite portable charger brands, Anker, also makes travel adapters. This one plugs into most European outlets to provide a single grounded US outlet, a USB-A port, and two USB-C ports. Unfortunately, the three USB ports max out at 15 watts total, so it’s best for overnight gadget charging, but I appreciate the temperature and overload protection. There is also a UK version ($16).

Sources indicate that epicka Hybrid European Travel Plug Adapter for $26: This handy adapter turns one outlet into four and includes four USB ports (two A and two C). It has fold-out Type A prongs, but you can also slide on a fold-out Type C plug for use in Europe. While the USB ports support QC 3.0 or PD 3.0, they max out at 20 watts in total. I prefer the OneBeat adapters recommended above.

You can do better than these travel adapters.

According to recent reports, EZQuest WorldTravel GaN 5 Port With PD Wall Charger: This travel adapter has a generous four USB-C ports and one USB-A port with a familiar slide-out prong design that covers more than 150 countries. There’s also a built-in 10-amp fuse and a spare. It has RoHS, CE, and FCC certification. It works fine, but it's kinda boxy, and the sliders don't lock in place as securely as some of our other picks. There's also a 65W version ($60).

In a recent development, rolling Square Pocket Travel Adapter: I admire any attempt to shrink down travel adapters in size, but the three-pronged UK plugs are usually the obstacle. Rolling Square’s solution is to have a flip-out third prong, but you’ll need a good fingernail to unhitch it. This charger has a single USB-C port capable of delivering up to 30 watts and is a compact option that covers the US, UK, and Europe.

Ceptics 65W World Travel Adapter.

Recent findings suggest that ceptics 65W World Travel Adapter: This versatile adapter comes with Type A, B, C, E/F, G, and I slide-on plugs. They fit onto the rectangular brick and plug directly into the outlet, or you can attach them to the optional five-foot cable. The brick has one grounded US outlet and a second non-grounded outlet, with one USB-A (30-watt) and two USB-C (65- and 33-watt) ports at the other end. It works fine, and it's affordable, but it's bulky and ugly.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for years, the case for quantum computing has rested on ambitious promises, from discovering newly introduced drugs by simulating how molecules behave to optimizing supply chains and airline schedules. Many of the biggest aims are still likely to be years, if not decades, away.

But quantum software, which uses algorithms designed to solve complex problems faster than conventional computers, is already being tested on a more immediate challenge: the energy transition, from keeping power grids stable to finding better materials for solar cells and hydrogen production.

Phasecraft, a quantum software company founded in Bristol, England, in 2019, is one of the firms putting the technology to work in energy. It raised $34 million in Series B funding in 2025, and in September this year declared intends to set up U.S. headquarters in Arlington, Virginia.

There are enormous opportunities to solve problems that are both crucial for energy security and commercially valuable, Ashley Montanaro, co-founder and CEO of Phasecraft, told CNBC.

Phasecraft isn't alone in applying quantum software to the energy industry.

Industry observers note that quantinuum, which was formed by the merger of Cambridge Quantum and Honeywell Quantum Solutions and listed on Nasdaq in June, is using the technology to model materials for hydrogen fuel cells for transportation. It is also working with partners on materials for carbon capture.

Industry observers note that another U.K. player, ORCA Computing, a spinout from the University of Oxford, has partnered with BP to better understand how a molecule's physical, chemical and biological properties are governed. That could help explain how biofuels burn and how to make them burn more efficiently.

In a separate project, ORCA worked with Japanese software manufacturer JIJ on a challenge power companies face: deciding which generators to switch on or off, and when, to meet demand at the lowest cost.

According to recent reports, that project also involved BP and the National Quantum Computing Centre (NQCC), the U.K.'s national laboratory for quantum computing, which is part of the government-backed U.K. Research and Innovation. The involvement of the NQCC, like that of ARPA-E, suggests governments are paying close attention to quantum software's potential role in energy, as are companies such as BP.

For Phasecraft, a priority is grid stability and optimization. It has partnered with the National Energy System Operator (NESO), the independent system planner that balances energy supply and demand in England, Scotland and Wales, on grid optimization tasks, including managing power exchanges and isolating network sections during emergencies. The manufacturer indicates its software can complete these tasks up to 1,000 times faster than conventional computing.

Phasecraft believes its grid software could be particularly sought after in Asia, where electrification is rapidly expanding, increasing the need for grid resilience to balance high and growing demand with the intermittent supply offered by renewables.

The tech giant is also working with U.K. solar cell maker Oxford PV on the development of new materials for photovoltaic cells capable of operating more efficiently than existing ones.

Industry observers note that separately, it has teamed up with London-listed specialty materials developer Johnson Matthey, Harvard University and Boston-based quantum hardware specialist QuEra, in work overseen by the U.S. government's Advanced Research Projects Agency–Energy (ARPA-E), to discover novel catalysts that would reduce reliance on scarce metals like iridium — which is presently critical in the production of hydrogen.

Asked why Phasecraft is focusing on energy rather than sectors that might seem more lucrative, Montanaro said the returns were there too.

"When you get this right, the commercial returns are real: more efficient energy networks mean lower operating costs and more value from existing infrastructure," he said.

Industry observers note that after we missed out on the Xiaomi 17 Pro and Pro Max last year, the Chinese smartphone giant is finally bringing its dual-screen flagships to the West. It's just rolled out the fresh Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, and I would be pretty worried if I were a certain Cupertino-based competitor.

Both phones look like an all-round excellent package, with top-of-the-line specs including the brand-upcoming Snapdragon 8 Elite chipsets.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro is the model for those after a more compact, but still powerful, phone, with its 6.4-inch 120Hz AMOLED front display and 6,000mAh battery. It's powered by the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chipset, paired with 12GB of RAM and either 256GB or 512GB of storage.

Sources indicate that the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, meanwhile, bumps the main screen size up to 6.9 inches and upgrades the chipset to the absolutely top-of-the-line Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 – currently the fastest Android SoC on the market. The base model offers 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, but there are also more expensive 12+512GB and 16+1TB versions available.

The bigger design also makes space for a much larger battery, which comes in at 7,050mAh with 100W wired HyperCharge support (the base 18 Pro, in contrast, only supports 90W wired HyperCharge).

The front displays of both phones support Xiaomi's fresh privacy display technology, which is effectively the company's take on Samsung's Privacy Display feature and helps obscure sensitive information from prying eyes.

Both the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max boast similar camera setups, with a 200MP main shooter and 200MP periscope telephoto lens alongside a 50MP ultra-wide. As with other recent Xiaomi devices, the cameras were co-engineered with Leica and offer a range of photo styles inspired by the camera maker.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

For me, the real highlight, however, is the innovative rear display situated on the back of both models. It offers a range of handy features, from controlling media playback to offering a real-time view of the cameras to make selfies easier.

You can fully customize it with a range of watch-like faces as well (including some options with cute 3D animal mascots) and even use generative AI to create your own apps right from the settings menu.

It's seriously cool and seems like a genuine reason to pick the 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max over other flagship models.

In a recent development, all of this doesn't exactly come cheap, however. The Xiaomi 18 Pro starts at £1,199 (that's roughly $1,600), and the 18 Pro Max starts at £1,399 (around $1,850) for the 12+256GB model.

They both come in four color options: Black, White, Velvet Red, and Cosmic Blue.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Voice is a wonderful service that’s often neglected, but with RCS supposedly on the way, a latest app redesign is now rolling out on Android that might as well have a major neon sign that says “RCS is coming.”.

According to recent reports, google Voice is a US-only service that operates a phone number over the internet. No normal carrier, just an app tied to your Google account that gets a phone number with the ability to make calls and send/receive text messages. The latter, though, has been a point of contention for the past few years as Voice was excluded from Google’s huge push into RCS.

That might finally be changing, though. Recent updates brought mention of RCS in the app’s code.

Now, a slightly newer version (v2026-11-01-1019342246) of Google Voice has debuted a redesign for the app on Android.

In a recent development, the new look isn’t a drastic restructuring, but a huge coat of paint on an app that hasn’t seen any meaningful updates since 2023. The new look feels more modern and very much influenced by Google Messages. The text field at the bottom has a rounded design with the same “+” and camera icons found in Messages, as well as a new long-press gesture that is, again, similar to Google’s primary messaging app. The main page hasn’t been updated beyond a new, rounded search bar up top and some subtly bolder fonts.

Material You colors are hit or miss now. On a Pixel with an orange theme, that color influenced the entire UI, but on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 with a coral/blue theme, the only sign of themeing was a blue message field.

The most crucial thing here is the “SMS” icon on the send button, which looks just like the button in Google Messages. In that app, it’s used as an indicator as to what type of message you’re sending – SMS or RCS. Combined with code in that other recent update directly pointing to “RCS” being used on a send button, you can absolutely tell Google Voice is finally adding this long-overdue functionality.

A timeline for RCS support in Google Voice is still unclear, but this redesign going live now certainly suggests it’s coming sooner rather than later.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iPad Pro is Apple's best tablet, but not everyone needs its power.

When choosing your next iPad, it's not a difficult decision if you know the base model works for your needs, or if you want a small tablet. But it's trickier to decide between the iPad Air and iPad Pro if you're using an iPad for work or creative pursuits. Is saving $450 and opting for the still-capable iPad Air something you'll regret in the future?

The iPad Air starts at $749 for the 11-inch model with 128GB of storage and an M4 processor, while the 11-inch M5 256GB base iPad Pro costs $1,199. Both devices offer 13-inch variants if you want a larger screen. Those prices might seem higher than you remember, due to the ongoing RAM crisis that's been spiking consumer tech prices. Apple hasn't been immune to its effects, and has passed those costs onto would-be iPad customers.

It has been revealed that while the iPad Pro packs plenty of improvements, its strongest selling point is what meets your eyes right away: the display. It also relies on a faster processor that makes a meaningful difference in intensive apps. Picking between it and the Air comes down to how you initiative to take advantage of the Pro's advanced spec sheet.

In a recent development, the iPad Air's laminated IPS LED display is great, with solid color accuracy, P3 wide color gamut support and a pixel density of 264 ppi that makes text crisp and clear to read. The iPad Pro also has a pixel density of 264 ppi, but that's where the similarities end.

At 1,000 nits and up to 1,600 nits with HDR, the Pro's brighter tandem OLED display is miles ahead of the Air's 500-nit display. It relies on two OLED panels stacked on each other to boost brightness and color accuracy. With a contrast ratio of 2,000,000:1, it has incredibly deep blacks, which are appreciated for video creation and consumption alike.

Its 120Hz ProMotion display also feels smoother as you work through app menus, play games or simply scroll through the interface. To conserve battery, it can drop down to 10Hz while displaying images or other static content like a webpage. To reduce reflections and hide smudges, Apple also offers a nano-texture glass option at an additional cost for the top-tier Pro models.

The latest iPad Air released in March 2026 and relies on Apple's M4 chip, while the Pro stepped up to an M5 in October 2025. To put that in context, the iPad Pro lineup used M4 back in 2024. The M4 processor is more than enough for most tasks, including gaming and video editing. It can handle rendering, media editing and on-device AI tools with no problem.

In a recent development, however, we found that the M5 in the iPad Pro was twice as fast when it came to running local AI models for advanced image generation tools. It offers 45 percent higher graphics performance and 15 percent faster multithreaded performance over the M4 processor.

It has been revealed that with the M5 chip, you'll shave off a couple of seconds across intensive tasks. Admittedly, these are niche use cases, but if you want the best hardware Apple offers, paying more for the Pro model saves you time across the experience. The uptick in performance also lets the iPad Pro drive external displays at 120Hz, while the Air is restricted to 60Hz.

Sources indicate that while the camera is seldom on the priority list when considering an iPad, the iPad Pro relies on some nifty tech uncommon among tablets. A Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) sensor next to the Pro models' rear camera helps with better autofocus and AR scanning.

Industry observers note that through third-party apps like Polycam, it can make floor maps of your home and develop 3D renders. Apple's Measure app lets the iPad Pro accurately measure item heights and the distance between objects, making it a great assistant when you're getting upcoming furniture or rearranging the house. While the iPad Air also has the Measure app, it lacks this sensor that enhances its accuracy.

According to recent reports, on the front, the Pro supports Face ID, letting you unlock your tablet without a password, while the iPad Air still relies on a fingerprint sensor for Touch ID. The advanced TrueDepth camera array also grants the ability to develop a spatial render of your face for Animoji and Memoji, or Portrait Mode selfies with background blur adjustments.

According to recent reports, the iPad Pro comes with twice the base storage (128GB vs. 256GB), plus quad speakers compared to the Air's stereo speaker setup. It also supports fast charging with a 60W power adapter (not included), while its Thunderbolt 3 / USB 4 USB-C port can transfer large files faster and drive external monitors at 120Hz. The Pros used to have more RAM than the Air models, but the M4 Air matches them with 12GB of unified memory.

The iPad Pro keeps these advantages in a body that's only 5.3mm (0.21 inches) deep, slimmer than the already impressive 6.1mm (0.24 inches) of the iPad Air. They offer the same 10 hours of battery life for web browsing and video streaming. Individually, these features may not mean much outside of specific purposes. But together, they can make a compelling argument for the cost.

Despite these advantages, there's not enough here for a casual user that would justify spending $450 more for the iPad Pro. At $749, the iPad Air strikes the right balance of performance and features despite Apple's price hike this year from its prior price of $599. If you aren't going to take advantage of the iPad Pro's extra horsepower for video and photo editing, or by making the iPad your primary work device, your needs will be served just as well by the more affordable iPad Air.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As previewed at I/O 2026, you can text — via Google Messages and iMessage — or email directly with Gemini.

Instead of using the Gemini app, you can now reach the AI assistant to “start tasks and get updates” using your preferred method of communication. To get started, go to gemini.google.com/channels.

You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries.

Text with Gemini works via Google Messages and iMessage. Google does note that this method is “not end-to-end encrypted and may be accessible by your carrier.” The setup process involves verifying a phone number. Existing numbers associated with your Google Account appear automatically, and there’s the ability to add a latest one.

Afterward, you’ll receive a text from Gemini via RCS Business Messaging that offers a pretty straightforward chat experience. Before sending, booking, or other “major actions,” Gemini will ask for 1-tap confirmation.

It has been revealed that …you can text a request, snap a photo of a school flyer to add dates to your Google Calendar, or get scheduled check-ins in a private 1:1 thread. If your plans change while Gemini is working, simply reply to the text to steer the task mid-run without starting over.

(Amusingly, Text with Gemini coexists with the existing Google Messages integration, which you can distinguish by the old blue/purple icon.).

Email with Gemini lets you “start tasks and get updates by emailing” gemini@google.com. Google explicitly names Gmail, Apple Mail, or Outlook as supported clients, while emails from Gemini are always “1:1 to you (never “Reply-All”) with a link to review and confirm your results.”.

Forward a batch of school emails to add key dates to Google Calendar, spot schedule conflicts, or send over threads and PDFs to sort out medical bills and track insurance renewals.

You can manage phone numbers and turn off both options from this new Channels page. If you’re more familiar with using your email client or phone’s messaging app, Text and Email with Gemini might boost your assistant usage. This is available first in the US.

Meanwhile, when revealed in May, these two options were intended for Gemini Spark, which has since been integrated into the main Gemini experience as “tasks.”.

Why does your phone say no service even with a SIM card?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If your calls and texts aren't going through, try these recommendations.
  • In a recent development, the modern electronic device has made a lot of strides in ensuring that it lets you know when something has gone awry.
  • Industry observers note that on your phone, you may notice one of these alerts in the form of a notification that notes, "No SIM card installed." This can be alarming, as it's possible that you may not know what a SIM card even does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your calls and texts aren't going through, try these recommendations.

In a recent development, the modern electronic device has made a lot of strides in ensuring that it lets you know when something has gone awry. Things like computers, game consoles and tablets will often find a way to alert you to an concern, which makes it easier to troubleshoot any potential problems that may arise.

Industry observers note that on your phone, you may notice one of these alerts in the form of a notification that notes, "No SIM card installed." This can be alarming, as it's possible that you may not know what a SIM card even does. Or if you do know what the SIM card does, it can lead to some worrying conclusions as you try to troubleshoot it.

Fixing a SIM card error is a task that requires some diagnostic detective work, or if you're extra unlucky, some actual physical work. Thankfully, there are a lot of tools, both in your phone's settings and in the real world, that can assist with a potential fix.

When a SIM card error leaves you without service, the phone will still work and power on; it will just be without its main features. The only thing that needs to be done is to take it out and put it right back in. This is usually caused by dropping the phone or ithe card not being properly seated when it was serviced for you, but you can use a SIM ejector tool to take it out. If you don't have one, something as simple as a paper clip or safety pin will usually do the trick.

It's always worth finding out if it's something as simple as a carrier outage, which is entirely possible. If you have access to another device on a different carrier and it can connect to the internet or make a phone call, that could indicate a network outage specific to your carrier. Asking a local friend or family member using the same service whether their phone is working properly can confirm a carrier outage or eliminate it as a possibility.

Your phone may be using an eSIM card, which replaces the physical card with a digital SIM. These are great, but they tend to have unique concerns with international travel. If you're using an eSIM card, the way you access settings on an iPhone is slightly different from Android. On an iPhone, eSIM cards are located in Cellular or Mobile Data in the Settings menu, while Android stores them in a setting called SIM Manager. By turning on data roaming, you may fix any sort of problems you're having.

In a recent development, A SIM card or "no service" error can sometimes be something at a software level as opposed to something being wrong with the card. One of the more common fixes is simply toggling airplane mode on and off. Airplane mode can be found by swiping down from the top of your phone and tapping the airplane button.

It has been revealed that you may also be able to do a quick network reset, which sounds bad but has zero effect on your personal files. Doing a network reset on an iPhone is largely similar to the process on Android. It should be noted, however, that the iPhone's network reset is in the Transfer or Reset section of Settings, while Android stores it in Reset Options, also in Settings. You will need to sign back into your Wi-Fi, however, along with some other connections.

According to recent reports, we all get busy in life, and if you haven't paid your bill, then your SIM card will simply stop connecting to your carrier's network. It may seem like a simple thing, but sometimes the simple solutions are blindingly obvious. If you pay your bill online, check your account to see if you've missed a payment or if your service hasn't been suspended for some other reason.

Industry observers note that getting no service on your phone may not even have anything to do with a bad SIM card or an inactive account. You may just be in a place with limited to no service available, or a cellphone tower may be blocked by something. Move around and look for someplace that you actually can connect, as the error may be a result of poor service in that area.

#2033. Six products and services Google discontinued in 2026
